_comment: ⚠ ONE CORPUS, TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS. The Go agent and the TypeScript extension both hand a
model-authored string to `sh -c`, and they need the same bound. The Go parser cannot be called
from TypeScript — separate runtimes, and compiling it to WASM to gate a VS Code extension's
shell calls would be a disproportionate amount of machinery on a security path. So the design is
ported, and THIS FILE is what keeps the two from drifting: both test suites read it and assert
the same verdict for every command. A divergence fails one side's build.
Both readers must fail loudly if this file is missing rather than scanning an empty set — a
guard whose corpus has moved passes unconditionally and proves nothing.
decision: allow = runs unattended | confirm = one prompt showing the exact command | refuse =
never runs, not even with confirmation, because nobody could know what they were agreeing to.

_comment: ⚠ WHAT THE BOUND COSTS SOMEONE DOING ORDINARY WORK, MEASURED ON BOTH SIDES. If the allow rate
on real agent work drops, the bound is on its way to being switched off — which is the same
outcome as not having one. 16 of these 20 must run unattended; the 4 that do not are writes,
deletes and reads outside the toolchain.
